subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Risk Aversion for Gains, Risk Seeking for Losses
description: A quick, practical guide to Risk Aversion for Gains, Risk Seeking for Losses.

hook.text: Win $500 for sure, or flip for $1,000? Most take the sure thing. Now reverse it with losses.

buildup.text: Lose $500 for sure, or flip for a chance to lose $1,000 or nothing? Most gamble. Same math, opposite behavior.

discovery.text: People are risk-averse when winning and risk-seeking when losing. The domain flips the preference.

twist.text: This is why people hold losing stocks hoping they'll recover, but sell winning stocks too early.

climax.text: Whether you're in gain or loss territory changes your entire risk appetite. It's automatic, not strategic.

punchline.text: Winning makes you cautious. Losing makes you reckless.

quiz.question: How does domain affect risk preferences?
options: Risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses

details.summary: Prospect theory reveals an asymmetry in risk preferences: people avoid risks when facing potential gains, preferring a sure thing, but seek risks when facing potential losses, preferring a gamble over a certain loss.
details.whyItMatters: This asymmetry explains seemingly contradictory behavior. The same person who takes the safe investment option will also double down on a losing position, because the psychological context of gains versus losses reverses risk tolerance.
takeaways: People prefer certain gains over risky ones with higher expected value
People prefer risky losses over certain ones with equal expected impact
The same person can be risk-averse and risk-seeking depending on domain

faq.question: Why do gamblers who are losing bet more aggressively?
faq.answer: In the loss domain, a certain loss feels unbearable due to loss aversion. A gamble offers hope of escaping the loss entirely. The possibility of returning to break-even is psychologically worth the risk of deeper losses.

faq.question: How does this asymmetry affect business decisions?
faq.answer: Companies in profitable positions tend to play it safe and avoid innovation risk. Companies facing losses take bigger gambles on turnaround strategies. This explains why struggling companies often make bold, sometimes reckless, moves.
